claims.text: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has a large caloric response.
The untreated alloy has poor mechanical integrity and tends to crack under service or operational fields.
Conventional processing produces a coarse microstructure in the alloy.
High-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering with approximately 5 vol% TiC will produce a refined nanocomposite microstructure.
The TiC nanoparticles will be distributed both along grain boundaries and within grains.
TiC nanoparticles will promote grain refinement.
TiC nanoparticles will obstruct crack propagation.
TiC reinforcement will improve load transfer in the alloy composite.
Impeded crack growth and improved load transfer will increase fracture toughness.
TiC is chemically inert under the proposed processing and operating conditions.
The thermal conductivity and chemical inertness of TiC will minimize interference with the field-induced martensitic transformation.
Approximately 5 vol% TiC will increase compressive strength by 25–50% relative to the untreated alloy.
Approximately 5 vol% TiC will enhance fracture toughness relative to the untreated alloy.
Approximately 5 vol% TiC will cause no detectable reduction in caloric-response magnitude.
Maintaining the TiC fraction near 5 vol% and optimizing milling and sintering parameters can preserve the intrinsic phase transformation.

contradictions.description: The boundary limits operation to elastic loading, whereas compressive-strength and fracture-toughness tests necessarily involve yielding, fracture, or crack propagation beyond the elastic regime.

The baseline is described as conventionally processed, while the intervention includes ball milling and spark plasma sintering; the experiment nevertheless says the conventional and TiC-containing samples are processed under identical conditions. It is therefore unclear whether the control is the unchanged conventional alloy or an alloy-only powder-metallurgy control.
